title: Mind: Its Mysteries and Control
author: Swami Sivananda
edition_cited: World Wide Web (WWW) Edition 1998 of the Twelfth Edition (1994), The Divine Life Society, 'This WWW reprint is for free distribution'; text from the copy mirrored at archive.org item mind-its-mysteries
locator_hints: Chapter 'Experiences and Obstacles in Meditation', headings 'EXPERIENCES IN MEDITATION' and 'Lights' (WWW ed. pp. 161-163; file lines c. 10030-10070): the divine ray like a sunbeam through a slit; colour of the lights depends on which tattva flows in the nostrils (agni red, akasa blue, apas white, prithvi yellow, vayu black) and can be changed by thought
Same chapter (file lines c. 10115-10135): a 'dazzling light with abrupt motion'; 'if you see a blazing light during meditation ... do not fall back in terror'
Chapter on Nirguna meditation (file lines c. 9588-9612): open-eyed gazing 'on the formless air', on the expansive sky; imagined infinite jyotis; trataka on Om
File line c. 9207: 'You will witness the splendid Antarjyotis ... Unmani Avastha' when the sushumna opens
summary: A companion to the Kundalini Yoga record, useful for two points not made there. First, Sivananda ties the colour of lights seen in meditation to the tattva said to be flowing in the breath at that moment (fire red, ether blue, water white, earth yellow, air black) and says the tattva, and so the colour, can be changed by thinking intently of another element. Second, he reassures those frightened by a sudden blazing or abruptly moving light: do not mistake it for a phantom, do not give up, 'break veil after veil'. Elsewhere in the book he prescribes open-eyed gazing at formless air or the wide sky as a nirguna meditation and trataka on a drawn Om until tears flow. The treatment is brief and mixed with general exhortation; nothing is said to the person who sees no light.
why_relevant: Supplementary teacher guidance on interpreting and responding to lights that arise, with a colour-to-breath claim and open-eyed sky gazing.
